scenes.visual: Title card 'What a Microscope Can Show' fades in over a cartoon brass compound microscope beside a thin, pale slice of cork. THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures. COLOUR MAP, the same in every scene and in the second film, and matching the lesson's size-ladder figure: EYE LIMIT = GREY dashed horizontal line with a small eye icon; LIGHT-MICROSCOPE LIMIT = GOLD solid line with a light-microscope icon; ELECTRON-MICROSCOPE LIMIT = PURPLE dashed line with an electron-microscope icon; DOTS and CELL WALLS = dark BLUE; BLUR = soft BLUE haze; a GAP COUNTER in the top-left corner reads the gap between the two dots in micrometers. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: In sixteen sixty-five, Robert Hooke saw rows of tiny boxes in a thin slice of cork. He called the boxes cells. What decides what a microscope can show? And why was seeing those boxes not enough? We start with the tool.
scenes.visual: A hand lifts an exceedingly thin slice off a cork block. Zoom into a round microscope view: rows of empty dark-BLUE walled boxes like a honeycomb, label '1665: Hooke's cork (schematic)'. Two question marks appear beside the view: 'what can a tool show?' and 'why was seeing not enough?'. The boxes stay on screen while the narrator speaks.
scenes.caption: In 1665, Robert Hooke saw rows of tiny boxes in a thin slice of cork. He called the boxes cells. What decides what a microscope can show? And why was seeing those boxes not enough? We start with the tool.
scenes.narration: In 1665, Robert Hooke saw rows of tiny boxes in a thin slice of cork. He called the boxes cells. What decides what a microscope can show? And why was seeing those boxes not enough? We start with the tool.

scenes.tts: Two words matter here. Magnification is how many times larger an image looks than the real object. Resolution is the smallest distance between two points at which you still see two separate points.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left, labelled 'magnification': a small dark-BLUE square grows to three times its size, with 'x1' then 'x3' on screen. Right, labelled 'resolution': two dark-BLUE dots with a double-headed arrow between them and the words 'smallest gap that still looks like two'. Both labels stay on screen.
scenes.narration: Two words matter here. Magnification is how many times larger an image looks than the real object. Resolution is the smallest distance between two points at which you still see two separate points.

scenes.tts: Watch two dots on a slide under an ordinary light microscope. A micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter. The dots start close together and look like one blur. Slowly they move apart. Near a gap of about zero point two micrometers, they begin to look like two.
scenes.caption: Watch two dots on a slide under an ordinary light microscope. A micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter. The dots start close together and look like one blur. Slowly they move apart. Near a gap of about 0.2 micrometers, they begin to look like two.
scenes.visual: A round light-microscope view. Two dots sit almost on top of each other inside one soft BLUE haze. The GAP COUNTER, top left, reads '0.05 µm' and climbs smoothly ('0.10 µm', '0.15 µm', ...) as the dots drift apart. A GOLD marker on the counter scale reads 'ordinary light microscope: limit about 0.2 µm'. The haze stays one blob, starts to pinch in the middle as the counter nears 0.2 µm, and by a little past it shows two separate hazes, each around one dot (a gradual change, not a sudden snap). On-screen note: '1 µm = 1/1000 mm'. Labelled 'schematic blur'.
scenes.narration: Watch two dots on a slide under an ordinary light microscope. A micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter. The dots start close together and look like one blur. Slowly they move apart. Near a gap of about 0.2 micrometers, they begin to look like two.

scenes.tts: Why the blur? Even a well-made ordinary light microscope blurs the finest details. Light spreads out as it passes through the opening of the lens. So each point becomes a small smudge, and close smudges merge into one.
scenes.visual: Side view, labelled 'schematic': straight light rays pass through the round opening of a cartoon lens and spread out slightly on the far side. Below, each dot grows a soft BLUE halo. Two halos slide together and overlap into one shape. Caption tag: 'even a well-made ordinary light microscope blurs the finest details'.
scenes.narration: Why the blur? Even a well-made ordinary light microscope blurs the finest details. Light spreads out as it passes through the opening of the lens. So each point becomes a small smudge, and close smudges merge into one.

scenes.tts: Now set the dots zero point one five micrometers apart. They look like one blur. We triple the magnification. Will you see one dot or two?
scenes.caption: Now set the dots 0.15 micrometers apart. They look like one blur. We triple the magnification. Will you see one dot or two?
scenes.visual: The microscope view again. GAP COUNTER fixed at '0.15 µm', below the GOLD 'limit 0.2 µm' marker. One BLUE haze. A magnification slider labelled 'x1' slides toward 'x3' and stops just before it. Big on-screen question: 'one dot or two?'
scenes.narration: Now set the dots 0.15 micrometers apart. They look like one blur. We triple the magnification. Will you see one dot or two?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame with the question 'one dot or two?' and a small 5-second countdown ring in the corner.

scenes.tts: Still one. The blur got bigger, and it is still one blur. Making the image bigger does not shrink the limit. Magnification makes an image bigger. Resolution decides how much detail it holds.
scenes.visual: The slider snaps to 'x3'. The whole view, haze and all, scales up to three times its size; it is still one BLUE blob. GAP COUNTER still reads '0.15 µm' and the GOLD marker still reads '0.2 µm'. Two lines write themselves on screen: 'magnification: bigger image' and 'resolution: how much detail'.
scenes.narration: Still one. The blur got bigger, and it is still one blur. Making the image bigger does not shrink the limit. Magnification makes an image bigger. Resolution decides how much detail it holds.

scenes.tts: So here is the rule. A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than the tool's limit. Enlarging the image adds no detail. A whole cell can be clear while its parts are not.
scenes.visual: The rule types out in a box in the centre: 'A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than the tool's limit.' Beneath it, a small BLUE blob is enlarged by a magnifying-glass icon and stays a blob, tagged 'enlarging adds no detail'. Then a cartoon cell outline appears beside the GOLD line: its outline is sharp, its inside is a soft haze, tagged 'cell: clear / parts: not' (schematic).
scenes.narration: So here is the rule. A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than the tool's limit. Enlarging the image adds no detail. A whole cell can be clear while its parts are not.

scenes.tts: Each tool has its own limit. Picture a ladder of sizes, each rung ten times smaller than the one above. Your eye's limit sits near a tenth of a millimeter. The light microscope's gold line sits far lower. The electron microscope's line sits lower still.
scenes.visual: A tall vertical ladder builds from the top, rungs labelled '1 mm', '100 µm', '10 µm', '1 µm', '0.1 µm', '10 nm', '1 nm' (each 'ten times smaller' tagged between two rungs). As each tool is named, its line slides across: GREY dashed eye line at 100 µm (0.1 mm), GOLD line at 0.2 µm, PURPLE dashed electron line between 1 nm and 10 nm, labelled '1 to 2 nm'. No objects are placed on the ladder in this scene.
scenes.narration: Each tool has its own limit. Picture a ladder of sizes, each rung ten times smaller than the one above. Your eye's limit sits near a tenth of a millimeter. The light microscope's gold line sits far lower. The electron microscope's line sits lower still.

scenes.tts: Hooke needed a microscope to make out the outlines and spacing of the cork boxes. Much smaller or low-contrast details inside cells needed better resolution, more contrast and later tools.
scenes.visual: One icon slides onto the ladder: a single dark-BLUE walled box labelled 'Hooke's cork cell (schematic position)', placed below the GREY eye line and well above the GOLD line. A short arrow from the eye icon to the box is crossed out; an arrow from the microscope icon to the box is drawn. The spacing between neighbouring walls is marked with a small double-headed arrow, tagged 'outlines and spacing'. The GOLD and PURPLE lines pulse briefly as the narrator says 'better resolution', and a small stain-dropper icon appears as the narrator says 'more contrast'. No other objects appear.
scenes.narration: Hooke needed a microscope to make out the outlines and spacing of the cork boxes. Much smaller or low-contrast details inside cells needed better resolution, more contrast and later tools.

scenes.tts: But look at what he had. Empty walls, left after the cork's cells had died. One material, from one kind of plant. That cannot show that all living things are made of cells.
scenes.visual: Back to the honeycomb view of cork. The boxes are drawn as empty outlines, tagged 'walls of dead cells'. A tag 'one material, one plant' appears. A thought bubble, 'all living things are made of cells?', appears beside it with a small grey 'not yet' stamp.
scenes.narration: But look at what he had. Empty walls, left after the cork's cells had died. One material, from one kind of plant. That cannot show that all living things are made of cells.

scenes.tts: Making out cells needs a tool with fine enough resolution. Building the theory needed more: comparing many kinds of living things, and testing where new cells come from. About one hundred seventy-five years passed before scientists argued that plants and animals alike are built of cells.
scenes.visual: Two columns build side by side. Left column 'making out cells': the GOLD line and the microscope icon. Right column 'building the theory': a stack of small panels, a leaf, a tadpole, a pond drop, each with cell outlines (schematic), and a question tag 'where do new cells come from?'. A timeline bar along the bottom runs from '1665' to '1838 to 1839' with '~175 years' over it.
scenes.caption: Making out cells needs a tool with fine enough resolution. Building the theory needed more: comparing many kinds of living things, and testing where new cells come from. About 175 years passed before scientists argued that plants and animals alike are built of cells.
scenes.narration: Making out cells needs a tool with fine enough resolution. Building the theory needed more: comparing many kinds of living things, and testing where new cells come from. About 175 years passed before scientists argued that plants and animals alike are built of cells.

scenes.visual: End card: the Hex mascot holding a small magnifying glass beside the line 'A detail shows only if it is larger than the tool's limit.' The GOLD limit line runs under the text.
